definition: In machine learning, grafting is a technique for improving the classification accuracy of a decision tree.
details: A decision tree is a model used to make predictions by following a flowchart-like structure of choices based on the data. After an initial, simple tree is built from a set of training data, grafting carefully adds new decision points or "branches" to it. This process aims to increase the tree's predictive accuracy by refining its logic, especially in areas where the original tree made mistakes. Grafting is the conceptual opposite of pruning, a more common technique where branches are removed from a complex tree to simplify it and prevent overfitting. While pruning makes a tree more general by reducing its complexity, grafting selectively adds complexity where it is predicted to improve results.

explainer.lead: Grafting improves a decision tree by adding carefully chosen branches after the first version has been built. It is useful when a simple tree makes recurring mistakes that a few extra decisions could correct, though added complexity must improve predictions rather than merely fit the training data.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting animals with a few questions, such as whether they can fly. If that rule keeps putting animals in the wrong groups, you can add another helpful question instead of starting over. Grafting means adding those extra questions to make the sorting guide more accurate.
tiers.practitioner: Apply grafting after building an initial tree by inspecting where its classifications fail and adding decision points that refine those regions. Compare the refined tree's predictive accuracy with the original before adopting it. The main pitfall is adding branches that correct training examples but overfit and fail to improve unseen cases.
tiers.paperLevel: Given an initial decision tree T trained on data D, grafting constructs T' by selectively adding decision nodes or branches to improve classification accuracy. It increases complexity locally, in contrast to pruning, which removes branches to simplify a tree. Its central limitation is that additions fitted to observed errors may overfit, so improved training accuracy alone does not establish better prediction.

explainer.example: Suppose a tree predicting customer cancellation uses only contract length and misclassifies 20 of 100 training customers who have short contracts. A graft adds a branch asking whether those customers contacted support, separating 12 of the mistaken cases into the correct class. The resulting tree is more complex but classifies 92 rather than 80 of those 100 training customers correctly.
explainer.intuition: A simple decision tree can divide data too coarsely, leaving some regions with repeated mistakes. Grafting treats those regions as places where a little extra decision logic may be worth adding.
howItWorks: Build an initial, relatively simple decision tree from training data.
Identify parts of the tree where its classifications are often wrong.
Add selected decision points or branches to refine those parts.
Keep the additions when they are predicted to improve predictive accuracy.
explainer.whyItMatters: Grafting offers a way to repair specific weaknesses without rebuilding or uniformly enlarging the whole tree. It also clarifies the trade-off between refining predictive logic and adding complexity that may not generalize.
misconceptions: Grafting is not pruning: it adds branches, while pruning removes them.
A more accurate tree on training data is not automatically more accurate on unseen data.
Grafting does not require making every part of the tree more complex; additions are selective.
